Rosse

GALAXIES, DRAWN BY HAND

Rosse builds galaxies in three dimensions and draws them entirely from hand-made marks: dots, strokes, stars and whole galaxies, drawn with a fineliner and cut out. Start from a type of galaxy, or any of the 239,695 in Galaxy Zoo 2; change its parts — arms, bar, bulge, dust — or what surrounds it: a merging neighbour, a lens, a foreground star. Drag to turn it; every view is drawn afresh.

About Rosse

Rosse is the drawing engine behind Almagest, a study of what a self-supervised encoder learns about galaxies. Almagest needed a way to show a galaxy that wasn’t a photograph — something that could draw what the encoder imagines as easily as what a telescope saw. So Rosse draws every galaxy from scratch, from a library of hand-made marks, at one pen weight, in full ink.

Each galaxy is built in three dimensions first: a bulge and a disc, arms with their spurs and clumps, a bar, rings, dust and a halo of stars. Mergers are simulated rather than drawn: two galaxies are set on their orbits, and their tidal tails come out of the physics. Lenses are traced through an elliptical mass, so rings, arcs and crosses appear where the geometry puts them, and change as you turn the view. Any Galaxy Zoo 2 galaxy can be drawn from its volunteers’ votes and its measured shape.

It is named after William Parsons, the third Earl of Rosse, who in 1845 became the first person to see a galaxy’s spiral arms, and drew them.
